text: The most common real-world security mistake in a new deployment isn't a sophisticated attack — it's a security rule written wide open during setup, to get something working fast, with a plan to tighten it later. This lesson covers why that promised cleanup rarely actually happens, and how to deploy the narrow rule from the start instead.

A rule like source-address-prefixes star, destination-port-ranges star, protocol star allows any traffic, on any port, from anywhere at all. It gets written so the engineer can stop fighting connectivity errors during setup and move on to the next task. Under real deadline pressure, the promised cleanup pass gets deprioritized, forgotten, or assumed to be someone else's job, and that rule quietly becomes the widest-open door into the network for the life of the deployment.

The fix is writing the narrow rule in the first place, not scheduling a cleanup for later. az network nsg rule create with a specific source range like 203.0.113.0/24 and port 443, or the AWS equivalent, aws ec2 authorize-security-group-ingress with that same CIDR and port, allows exactly one thing and nothing more. Both NSGs and security groups deny everything else by default — and it's the same number of commands as the wide-open version, just with the real values filled in instead of a wildcard.

Lesson 6 built three subnets specifically so each tier gets its own rules: nsg-web allows port 443 from a known range, nsg-app allows the app port only from the web subnet's range, and nsg-data allows the database port only from the app subnet's range. A single wide-open NSG attached to everything collapses that whole design — the data tier that was supposed to be reachable only from the app tier ends up reachable from anywhere.
Next up: proving those rules actually behave the way they're written on paper, by verifying connectivity in both directions before building anything else on top of this network.
